title: Ephesus: The Spirit, Magic, and the Riot for Artemis
summary: At Ephesus Paul meets about twelve disciples who know only John's baptism; he baptizes them in the name of Jesus, and the Spirit comes on them. He teaches for two years in the lecture hall of Tyrannus, extraordinary miracles occur, would-be exorcists are routed, and new believers burn their costly books of magic. When the silversmith Demetrius sees his trade in shrines of Artemis threatened, he stirs up a riot in the theater, which the city clerk finally quiets.
story: This chapter covers the heart of Paul's third missionary trip, which is less a trip than a long residence in one of the great cities of the empire. Ephesus becomes the base from which the word of the Lord reaches the whole province of Asia; churches such as those at Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis were probably founded in this period by Paul's coworkers (compare Colossians 1:7; 4:13). In verse 21 the story turns: Paul resolves in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem and then to Rome. From here to the end of Acts, the plot moves toward those two cities, and the riot at Ephesus is the last great public scene of Paul's free ministry.
historical:
Ephesus, on the west coast of Asia Minor, was the leading city of the Roman province of Asia and the seat of its proconsul, with a population often estimated at well over a hundred thousand. Its temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, a vast building that drew pilgrims and also served as a bank. The city's great theater, still standing, held perhaps 20,000 to 25,000 people. Paul stayed about three years (20:31), probably from about AD 52 or 53 to 55 or 56, and during this time wrote 1 Corinthians (1 Corinthians 16:8-9).

Luke's titles for officials are strikingly precise. The Asiarchs of verse 31 (officials of the province of Asia) were prominent men connected with the provincial council, which among other things promoted the cult of Rome and the emperor; their exact functions are still debated, but the title is well attested in inscriptions. The city clerk was the chief civic officer, who drafted decrees and answered to Rome for public order, which explains his anxiety about a charge of rioting. Ephesus proudly called itself neokoros, temple guardian, of Artemis, a title found on its inscriptions and coins. The legal assembly of verse 39 refers to the regular citizen assembly, as opposed to this unlawful gathering.
cultural:
Ephesus was famous for magic. Ephesian letters, written spells and formulas, were known across the Greco-Roman world, and people bought scrolls of incantations to protect themselves, heal, curse, or win love. That background explains the burning of books worth fifty thousand drachmas (a drachma was roughly a day's wage for a laborer), an enormous sum. It also explains the scene with the seven sons of Sceva. Exorcists commonly invoked the names of powerful beings, and these men tried to use Jesus's name as a spell. No Jewish high priest named Sceva is known; he may have belonged to a high-priestly family, or the title may have been a self-promoting claim.

The Artemis worshiped at Ephesus was not quite the Greek huntress of mythology but a mother goddess whose cult statue, covered in rounded shapes whose meaning is debated, was believed to have fallen from heaven. Silver shrines were small models of her temple or image, sold to pilgrims and worshipers. Demetrius's speech mixes piety and profit honestly: the gospel threatens both his business and his goddess. The two-hour chant, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians, has the rhythm of a real acclamation.
literary: Luke organizes the chapter around the power of the name of the Lord Jesus. The first scene (verses 1-7) shows the Spirit given in that name; the second (verses 8-12) summarizes teaching and miracles; the third (verses 13-20) shows that the name cannot be used by those who do not belong to Jesus, and it ends with a growth summary. After the turning point of verse 21, the riot (verses 23-41) is told with vivid detail and irony: a crowd in confusion, most of whom did not even know why they were there, and a pagan official who ends up declaring that Paul's companions are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers. As in Philippi and Corinth, the officials of the empire find no crime in the Christians.

outline.t: Disciples of John receive the Spirit
Two years in the lecture hall of Tyrannus
The sons of Sceva and the burning of magic books
Paul resolves to go to Jerusalem and Rome
Demetrius and the riot in the theater
The city clerk dismisses the assembly

doctrines.note: Paul's first question at Ephesus is whether these disciples received the Holy Spirit. The Spirit's coming, marked here by tongues and prophecy, confirms their inclusion in the people of the risen Jesus.

Believers come forward confessing their deeds and burn their magic books at great cost. Repentance here is public, concrete, and expensive: it touches money, habits, and the sources of security people had trusted.

Demetrius reports Paul's message accurately: man-made gods are no gods at all. The chapter shows how idolatry is bound up with economics and civic identity, and why the gospel's challenge to it provokes such a reaction.

words.note: Hodos, way or road. In Acts, the Way is an early name for the Christian movement (9:2; 19:9, 23; 24:14). It pictures faith as a path walked with others, a whole way of life rather than only a set of opinions.

Asiarches, Asiarch, an official of the province of Asia. Asiarchs were wealthy, prominent men tied to the provincial council and its public festivals. That some of them were Paul's friends shows that his message had reached influential circles, and that they valued his safety.

Neokoros, temple keeper or guardian, used only here in the New Testament. Cities competed for this title as a mark of honor. The clerk uses it to remind the crowd that Ephesus's standing depends on keeping order, not on shouting.

Periergos, literally working around, used of busybodies and, as here, of magic arts, the meddling with hidden powers. The same word describes busybodies in 1 Timothy 5:13. Those who practiced it gave it up publicly.

christ: The name of the Lord Jesus is the thread through the chapter. Believers are baptized into it, the Spirit comes through it, extraordinary healings accompany its proclamation, and it cannot be used as a spell by people who do not know him. The evil spirit's reply to the sons of Sceva (Jesus I know) testifies that even hostile powers recognize his authority, echoing the Gospels, where demons recognized Jesus. The result is that the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor (verse 17). Christ is shown as Lord over the spiritual powers people feared and over the religious economy that depended on them, which is why his gospel reshaped a city.

hard.q: Were the twelve at Ephesus already Christians, and does this chapter teach a second experience of the Spirit after conversion?
hard.a:
The men are called disciples, but they had received only John's baptism and had not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit. Paul explains that John pointed to Jesus, baptizes them in Jesus's name, and lays hands on them, and the Spirit comes.

Pentecostal and charismatic Christians often read this and similar passages (Acts 8:14-17) as showing that believers may receive a baptism in the Spirit, marked by gifts such as tongues, as a distinct experience after conversion. Many other Christians read the twelve as disciples of John rather than of Jesus: their faith was incomplete until they heard and believed in Jesus, and their baptism and reception of the Spirit together mark their full conversion, not a second stage. On this view the unusual timing in Acts belongs to the transition from John's ministry to the church's. Catholic, Orthodox, and Anglican traditions also connect the laying on of hands here with confirmation. Christians agree that every believer receives the Spirit (Romans 8:9) and differ on how Acts' narratives describe the normal pattern; this is a second-order question.

questions: The new believers at Ephesus burned books worth a fortune. What would it mean for you to let go of something costly that competes with trust in Christ?
The sons of Sceva tried to use Jesus's name without knowing him. How do people today treat Jesus as a tool rather than a Lord?
Demetrius saw that the gospel threatened his income. Where does faith in Christ challenge the economic habits of your own world?
